questions.question: Why did the approval rate for debit cards in Colombia drop on 13 August 2026?
questions.answer:
## Routing Change to Acquirer B Caused 10.95pp Drop in Approval Rate

The approval rate for Colombian debit cards dropped **7.33 percentage points** on August 13, 2026 (from a 28-day baseline of 86.7% to 79.4%), due to a routing change that sent 100% of traffic to Acquirer B, which had significantly worse performance than the previous acquirer.[1]

### What Happened

At **14:00 local time on August 13**, routing version 14 (CHG-0813) was deployed, redirecting all Colombian domestic debit traffic to Acquirer B for cost optimization (targeting a 40 basis point fee reduction). The change remained active for **22 hours and 10 minutes** until it was rolled back at 12:10 on August 14 (CHG-0814).[2]**Production changes around August 13 in Colombia**

| change_id | changed_at_utc | changed_at_bogota | change_type | scope | description | timing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CHG-0813 | 2026-08-13T19:00:00.000Z | 2026-08-13T14:00:00.000Z | routing | CO | Routing v14: 100% of CO domestic debit to Acquirer B (cost optimization, -40 bps) | during Aug 13 |
| CHG-0814 | 2026-08-14T17:10:00.000Z | 2026-08-14T12:10:00.000Z | rollback | CO | Rollback routing v14 -> v13 (incident INC-0814) | after |
| CHG-0815 | 2026-08-15T13:00:00.000Z | 2026-08-15T08:00:00.000Z | decline_mapping | B | Mapping hotfix v2.3.1: R05 reclassified as soft and retryable | after |### Impact

During the incident window (Aug 13 14:00 to Aug 14 12:10):
- **Final approval rate dropped 10.95 percentage points** (from 86.5% baseline to 75.6%)
- **First-attempt approval rate dropped 13.8 percentage points** (from 84.6% to 70.7%)
- **110 lost approvals** out of 1,004 payments processed
- **$6,354 in lost approved volume**
- **$1,186 in fees paid** during the incident[3]**Impact of the routing change window**

| started_by | ended_by | window_payments | baseline_payments | baseline_first_attempt_rate | window_first_attempt_rate | baseline_final_rate | window_final_rate | final_rate_change_pp | window_approvals | expected_approvals_at_baseline | lost_approvals | window_attempted_usd | window_approved_usd | lost_approved_usd | window_fees_usd |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CHG-0813 | CHG-0814 | 1004 | 15182 | 0.8456 | 0.7072 | 0.8654 | 0.756 | -10.95 | 759 | 869.0 | 110.0 | 61689.16 | 47095.86 | 6354.2 | 1186.03 |### Root Cause: Acquirer B's Poor Performance

**Acquirer B had zero Colombian debit traffic in the baseline** — all traffic went to Acquirer A, which maintained an 86.5% final approval rate. When routing v14 switched 100% of traffic to Acquirer B, the entire segment's performance collapsed.[4]**Baseline acquirer performance (14 days before routing change)**

| acquirer_id | first_attempt_approval_rate | final_approval_rate | payments_sent | pct_of_traffic |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 0.8459 | 0.8653 | 15237 | 100.00 |The key problem was **decline code 05 ("Do not honor")** from Acquirer B:
- **137 failures with code 05** during the window (13.7% of all payments)
- This represented a **9.51 percentage point increase** vs. the baseline across all acquirers (4.1% → 13.7%)
- Code 05 was **mapped as "hard" and not retryable** in mapping version v2.3, meaning these failures could not be recovered through cascading to another acquirer[5]**Decline codes that grew during the drop**

| acquirer_id | reason_code | reason | baseline_failures | window_failures | baseline_pct_of_payments | window_pct_of_payments | delta_pp | all_acquirers_baseline_pct | all_acquirers_window_pct | all_acquirers_delta_pp |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B | 05 | Do not honor | 0 | 137 | 0.0 | 13.65 | 13.65 | 4.14 | 13.65 | 9.51 |
| B | 1A | Additional authentication required (3DS) | 0 | 52 | 0.0 | 5.18 | 5.18 | 1.1 | 5.18 | 4.08 |
| B | 91 | Issuer or switch unavailable | 0 | 12 | 0.0 | 1.2 | 1.2 | 0.47 | 1.2 | 0.72 |
| B | 51 | Insufficient funds | 0 | 38 | 0.0 | 3.78 | 3.78 | 4.2 | 3.78 | -0.42 |Other significant decline codes from Acquirer B:
- **Code 1A** (Additional authentication required): 52 failures (5.2% of payments), but these were retryable and recovered 53.8% through cascading
- **Code 51** (Insufficient funds): 38 failures (3.8%), mapped as soft but not retryable (policy decision)
- **Code 91** (Issuer unavailable): 12 failures (1.2%), retryable with 33.3% recovery[6]

### Evidence

The fn_approval_drivers analysis confirms Acquirer B drove the entire drop, contributing **-10.95 percentage points** through rate effect (its 75.6% approval rate vs. the 86.5% baseline). All other dimensions (issuers, card brands, merchant segments) showed proportional degradation consistent with being routed through a worse-performing acquirer.[4]

### Recovery

The incident ended when routing was rolled back from v14 to v13 at 12:10 on August 14, restoring traffic to Acquirer A. Approval rates recovered immediately, returning to 86.4% by the end of August 14.[2]

A subsequent mapping hotfix (CHG-0815) on August 15 reclassified code 05 as "soft and retryable" for Acquirer B, which would have allowed cascade recovery had the routing change remained in place.

### Recommended Actions

1. **Never route to an untested acquirer at 100% volume** — Acquirer B had no historical Colombian debit traffic to validate performance before the full cutover
2. **Review decline code 05 mapping** — The "hard, non-retryable" classification prevented cascade recovery of 137 failures that may have been retryable
3. **Validate cost savings against approval rate impact** — The 40 bps fee reduction was outweighed by the $6,354 in lost volume over just 22 hours
4. **Implement gradual rollouts** — Test new acquirer routing at 10-20% traffic before full migration

questions.question: Why did conversion in Brazil fall on 18 and 19 June 2026?
questions.answer:
## Brazil Conversion Drop Caused by Overly Aggressive Risk Rule

Brazil's conversion rate fell **2.65 percentage points** on June 18-19, 2026, dropping from 85.2% (baseline) to 82.6%. This was caused by an **overly aggressive risk rule** that blocked legitimate payments, not by approval rate problems.

### Impact

Over the two-day period (June 18-19):
- **131 lost conversions** due to excess risk blocks
- **128 excess blocks** compared to baseline behavior
- Risk block rate jumped from 0.9% to 3.5% (+2.6 pp)
- Approval rates for payments that cleared risk remained stable at ~87-88% [1]**Impact of risk rule change on conversion**

| baseline_intents | baseline_blocked | baseline_risk_block_rate | baseline_conversion_rate | window_intents | window_blocked | window_risk_block_rate | window_conversion_rate | risk_block_rate_change_pp | conversion_rate_change_pp | excess_blocks | lost_conversions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6418 | 60 | 0.0093 | 0.8524 | 4927 | 174 | 0.0353 | 0.8259 | 2.6 | -2.65 | 128.0 | 131.0 |### Root Cause

**CHG-0618** deployed on June 18 at 9:00 AM introduced "Risk rules v3: new card-velocity rule" that was too restrictive. The funnel data shows the problem was at the risk layer, not downstream at acquirers:
- June 17 (before): 21 risk blocks out of 2,057 intents (1.0%)
- June 18 (after): 69 risk blocks out of 2,332 intents (3.0%)
- June 19 (peak): 105 risk blocks out of 2,595 intents (4.1%) [2]

### Resolution

**CHG-0620** deployed on June 20 at 3:00 PM tuned the velocity threshold after review. Conversion recovered immediately:
- June 20 risk block rate: 2.2% (down from 4.1%)
- June 20 conversion rate: 86.1% (recovered from 81.8%) [3]

### Evidence

The hourly data confirms the drop started precisely when CHG-0618 deployed at 9:00 AM on June 18, and approval rates of payments that made it through risk screening remained healthy throughout the incident (87-88%), proving the issue was upstream at the risk layer, not at the acquirers. [4]

### Recommendation

Review the velocity rule's initial threshold setting. The rule correctly identified a fraud pattern but was calibrated too aggressively, blocking ~128 legitimate payments over two days before being tuned.

questions.question: Was there any early warning before the Colombia debit incident of 13 August 2026?
questions.answer:
## Yes, there was a clear early warning 7 days before the incident

**Cascade alerts flagged a critical issue on 6 August 2026**, a full week before the Colombia debit incident on 13 August. The alert system detected that Acquirer B had stopped retrying "Do not honor" (code 05) declines, which historically had a 100% cascade rate.

### The Early Warning Timeline

**6 August 2026** — First cascade alert triggered[1]
- Acquirer B's cascade rate for code 05 dropped from 100% baseline to just 5% (1 out of 20 failures cascaded)
- This was caused by decline-mapping change **CHG-0806** deployed at 08:00 Bogota time, which reclassified code 05 from "soft/retryable" to "hard/non-retryable" under mapping v2.3[2]

**7-12 August** — Alerts continued daily[3]
- Cascade rate remained at 0% for 6 consecutive days
- Code 05 failures ranged from 14-27 per day with zero retries
- No action was taken during this warning period

**13 August 2026** — The incident occurred[4]
- Routing change **CHG-0813** at 14:00 shifted 100% of CO domestic debit traffic to Acquirer B (previously all traffic went to Acquirer A)
- Final approval rate dropped to **79.4%** from an 86.7% baseline (−7.3 pp)[5]
- Code 05 failures spiked to 141 attempts with zero cascades, all marked non-retryable[2]**Cascade alerts for Colombia in early August**

| business_date | acquirer_id | first_reason_code | failures | cascaded | cascade_rate | baseline_cascade_rate | is_alert |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-08-06 | B | 05 | 20 | 1 | 0.05 | 1.0 | true |
| 2026-08-07 | B | 05 | 16 | 0 | 0.0 | 1.0 | true |
| 2026-08-08 | B | 05 | 14 | 0 | 0.0 | 1.0 | true |
| 2026-08-09 | B | 05 | 20 | 0 | 0.0 | 1.0 | true |
| 2026-08-10 | B | 05 | 27 | 0 | 0.0 | 1.0 | true |
| 2026-08-11 | B | 05 | 23 | 0 | 0.0 | 1.0 | true |
| 2026-08-12 | B | 05 | 24 | 0 | 0.0 | 1.0 | true |
| 2026-08-13 | B | 05 | 109 | 0 | 0.0 | 1.0 | true |
| 2026-08-14 | B | 05 | 60 | 0 | 0.0 | 1.0 | true |### What the Alert Caught

The cascade alert system correctly identified that the **6 August decline-mapping change broke the retry mechanism** for Acquirer B's code 05 responses. While Acquirer B carried minimal traffic before 13 August (all traffic was on Acquirer A), the alert warned that code 05 would not cascade if traffic shifted to B.

When the routing change on 13 August moved all debit traffic to Acquirer B, the latent issue became a production incident — the system could no longer recover "Do not honor" declines through cascades to another acquirer.

### Recommended Action

The early warning system worked as designed. The gap was in **alert response**: 7 days of consecutive cascade alerts should have triggered either:
1. Rollback of CHG-0806 (the mapping change), or  
2. Blocking the routing change CHG-0813 until the cascade issue was resolved

The incident was eventually mitigated by **CHG-0814** on 14 August, which rolled back the routing change.[6]

extra_samples.question: Why did the approval rate for debit cards in Colombia drop on 13 August 2026?
extra_samples.answer:
## Routing Change Sent 100% of CO Debit Traffic to Underperforming Acquirer B

The approval rate for Colombia debit cards dropped **10.95 percentage points** on August 13, 2026, from a baseline of 86.5% to 75.6% during the incident. [2]

### What Happened

At 14:00 local time on August 13, routing change **CHG-0813** redirected 100% of Colombia domestic debit traffic to Acquirer B for cost optimization (saving 40 basis points in fees). The drop lasted 22 hours until a rollback (**CHG-0814**) at 12:10 on August 14 restored routing to version 13. [1]

### Impact

**Window: August 13 14:00 to August 14 12:10**
- **110 lost approvals** (759 approved vs. 869 expected at baseline rate)
- **$6,354 in lost approved volume**
- **$1,186 in fees paid** during the incident
- Final approval rate dropped from 86.5% to 75.6% (-10.95 pp)
- First-attempt approval rate dropped from 84.6% to 70.7% (-13.8 pp)

[2]

### Root Cause

**Acquirer B had structurally lower approval rates than Acquirer A and a broken decline-code mapping for code 05.**

During the baseline period (July 30 - August 12), Acquirer A handled 100% of CO debit traffic with an 86.5% final approval rate. [3] When routing switched all traffic to Acquirer B, the entire -10.95 pp drop was attributable to Acquirer B's lower performance. [4]

**The primary driver was decline code 05 ("Do not honor"):**
- Code 05 grew from 4.14% of payments (on Acquirer A) to **13.65% on Acquirer B** (+9.51 pp across all acquirers)
- During the incident window, Acquirer B returned **137 code 05 failures** with a **0% cascade rate** — none were retried
- The decline mapping (v2.3) classified code 05 as **hard and not retryable**, preventing any recovery through cascades

[5] [6]

**Early Warning Signs Were Present:**

Cascade alerts for Acquirer B code 05 had been firing since **August 6** — a full week before the routing change. The alert showed that code 05's cascade rate collapsed from 100% (baseline) to 0% starting August 6, when decline-mapping v2.3 was deployed (**CHG-0806**). This mapping change added R65 handling but inadvertently broke code 05 retry logic. [7]

## Yes – Cascade Alerts Flagged the Problem 7 Days Before the Incident

**The cascade alert system detected the issue on August 6, 2026**, a full week before the Colombia debit incident on August 13. The alert warned that Acquirer B had stopped cascading decline code 05 (Do Not Honor), which became critical when routing changes sent all Colombia debit traffic to that acquirer.

### Early Warning Timeline

**August 6, 2026** – First cascade alert triggered for Acquirer B on decline code 05[1]
- Cascade rate collapsed from 100% (baseline) to 5% (1 out of 20 failures)
- Caused by decline-code mapping v2.3 deployed at 08:00 local time (CHG-0806)[2]

The **decline-code mapping change (CHG-0806)** on August 6 modified how Acquirer B handled code 05, preventing retries to other acquirers.
